reader.summary: Brazil's week was dominated by the tight presidential runoff between the Bolsonaro camp and Lula, with multiple polls showing a narrow Bolsonaro or Flavio Bolsonaro lead. The Senate delivered Lula a major legislative win by approving a shorter five-day workweek, a campaign promise that energized his base ahead of the runoff. Simultaneously, Brazil announced that Amazon deforestation had fallen to its lowest level since 1988, a historic environmental milestone credited to Lula's policies but also a key issue in the race. A storm broke over Meta after Brazil's electoral court found the platform exhibited anti-Lula algorithmic bias, and Lula's party announced it would take the case to the OAS. In the Amazon, a surge of wildfires prompted a government investigation into whether the fires were criminal or coordinated, adding urgency to the environmental debate. On the economic front, US tariffs struck Brazil's manufacturing sector while market euphoria masked a growing public-debt concern. The incoming right-wing Congress also moved to challenge the judge who previously jailed Bolsonaro, signalling post-election political battles to come.

key_events.event: Brazil confirmed Amazon deforestation fell to its lowest level since 1988, a record for the region.
Multiple polls showed Bolsonaro or Flavio Bolsonaro holding a narrow lead over Lula ahead of the presidential runoff.
The Brazilian Senate approved a bill shortening the standard workweek from six to five days, a key campaign promise of Lula.
Brazil's electoral court ruled that Meta exhibited algorithmic bias against Lula, and the platform's employees told Folha that his accounts were deliberately hindered.
A surge in Amazon wildfires prompted the government to investigate whether the fires were criminal or coordinated.
US tariffs hit Brazil's manufacturing hub, complicating the economic picture ahead of the runoff.
Brazil's incoming right-wing Congress signaled it would challenge the judge who jailed Bolsonaro, foreshadowing post-election clashes.
Lula pledged free weekend public transit nationwide and defended cutting the criminal-responsibility age to 16 for heinous crimes to shore up his campaign.

display.eli5:
Here's what's happening: Brazil is about to hold its second-round presidential vote, and the race is so close that a single rally or a single scandal could flip it. Lula and the Bolsonaro camp are both throwing everything they have at the road and the TV this week. This is the runoff final campaign sprint, and every headline is about who is winning the last few votes.

Why does this matter? Because whoever wins gets to run the country, control the Amazon, and decide whether the economy heads one direction or another. The Amazon just hit its lowest deforestation number in four decades, and both sides are claiming credit or blaming each other. The government is also investigating whether a surge in Amazon fires was criminal or coordinated, and both camps will use that finding as a weapon in their final speeches.

What will probably happen next? The Meta social-media case will get filed with the OAS as a formal complaint, and a Brazilian court will order Meta to treat both candidates equally before the vote. Meanwhile, the Senate's new shorter workweek will stop being a headline and just become a bumper sticker at rallies.

What would be a surprise? If the Banco Master bank scandal suddenly names a big name from the Bolsonaro team, that would shake things up badly with so little time before the vote. Most people are not expecting that.
